transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
Bomb-making material stockpiled at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant for nearly 20 years
is destroyed.
After public health concerns prompted three delays, NPR's Quill Lawrence reports the
Army carried out a controlled detonation in Middletown.
It's thousands of pounds of lead azide, which is an explosive the military has used since
World War I.
They moved it to this bunker in Iowa about 17 years ago, but then they noticed just this
past March that it had gotten too unstable to move.
Essentially, it had crystallized instead of being in liquid form.
If one of those crystals breaks, it could all blow up spontaneously.
The cold weather and the hot and cold fluctuations are making that more possible.
Since March, the Army and other agencies have been trying to figure out what to do.
Without really telling the wider public until last week.
Lucy Gue lives in Burlington.
She says people had masks and gloves to use after the detonation.
The ammunition plant spokesperson said, "Just hose everything down and it'll go away.
It'll be fine."
Or, "Just wipe it down with a baby wipe."
No problem.
And there was nothing said about PPE.
So yeah, people are completely unprepared.
Kilmar Abrego-Garcia, Salvadoran national targeted by the administration, has self-deported
to Spain, more from NPR's Julianna Kim.
Abrego-Garcia arrived in Madrid in a white cap and hoodie, according to footage from
the Associated Press.
Over the past year, the Trump administration sought to re-deport him after immigration
officials admitted that the first attempt was by mistake.
His lawyer says the move to Madrid was Abrego-Garcia's way of leaving on his own terms, and not by
the administration's.
The Department of Homeland Security celebrated his departure.
Meanwhile, Abrego-Garcia's attorney says the exit is temporary, given that his wife and
child are U.S. citizens.
He hopes to return to his family in Maryland after President Trump leaves office.
Julianna Kim, NPR News.
The FBI's deputy director, Chris Rea, is planning to retire around the end of the year.
Rea is the third person to leave the number two job at the bureau during the Trump administration,
and PR's Ryan Lucas has details.
Chris Rea has been serving as deputy director for less than a year.
He was put in the job after right-wing podcast host Dan Bongino left the post early this
year.
Rea then served as co-deputy director alongside former Missouri Attorney General Andrew Bailey
before Bailey stepped down this fall.
Unlike Bongino and Bailey, Rea is a career FBI agent who rose up through the ranks.
He was viewed by many inside the bureau as a steadying presence amid all the turmoil
under FBI Director Kash Patel, neither the FBI nor Patel has commented on Rea's planned
departure.
Ryan Lucas, NPR News, Washington.
U.S. stocks are sharply lower this hour with the Dow down 469 points.
This is NPR News.
NPR has confirmed that U.S. intelligence officials briefed congressional staff about collected
intelligence related to Alice Wang, the Chinese woman who had an affair with NVIDIA Chief
Jensen Wang.
The briefer said there is no evidence that Alice Wang herself is a Chinese spy or asset
of the country's intelligence services.
The briefer said there is more evidence that her associate, Kang Wei, sometimes described
as her husband or business partner as well, has ties to China's Ministry of State Security.
The Iraqi government has announced a major move to take back control of important oil
fields operated by the country's Kurdish regional government.
NPR's Jana Raf reports it widens the rift between Baghdad and Iraq's Kurdistan region.
The Iraqi government says the move is part of a crackdown across the country on oil smuggling.
Baghdad and the semi-autonomous Kurdistan region have long disagreed over the share
of oil revenue going to the Kurds.
Now Prime Minister Ali Azadi says the federal ministry will manage some of the biggest fields
under Kurdish control.
He has also directed that Kurdish checkpoints between federal government-controlled Iraq
and the Kurdish provinces be dismantled.
Kurdish leaders have rejected the moves and rejected allegations of oil smuggling.
Jana Raf, NPR News, Amman.
The White House is proposing new tariffs on the European Union in 13 countries, including
China and Japan.
I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News.

topics.text: Army detonates thousands of pounds of unstable lead azide stored at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant
Kilmar Abrego-Garcia self-deports to Madrid, Spain, after Trump administration's re-deportation push
FBI Deputy Director Chris Rea plans to retire at year's end, third to leave the post
U.S. stocks fall sharply, with the Dow down 469 points
U.S. intelligence briefs congressional staff on intelligence tied to Alice Wang and associate Kang Wei
Iraqi government moves to take control of major oil fields operated by Kurdish regional government
White House proposes new tariffs on European Union and 13 other countries, including China and Japan
